The COA on Your Peptide Probably Means Nothing

A polished PDF can create the appearance of certainty. Evidence begins only when the report can be tied to the vial, the laboratory can be independently identified, the methods answer the right questions, and the underlying output is available for review.

Novüm Research Team9 min readRUO
In this guideThe chain of evidenceDifferent testsRaw dataRed flagsFive-step audit

A certificate of analysis is not valuable because it is called a certificate. It is valuable when it records a real test performed on a traceable sample and gives an independent reviewer enough information to verify what happened. Remove any link in that chain and the document becomes a design asset, not scientific evidence.

Key principle
  • The lot on the vial must match the lot on the report.
  • Identity, chromatographic purity, and net peptide content answer different questions.
  • A report should expose the issuing laboratory, method, date, and authorisation.
  • Independent verification is stronger than a PDF hosted only by the seller.

The chain of evidence starts with the sample

The report must describe the item actually tested. That sounds obvious, yet many vendor certificates show a product name and a purity number with no defensible connection to the current lot. At minimum, look for a unique sample or report identifier, product identity, lot number, receipt or test date, and enough sample description to distinguish one material from another.

Next comes the laboratory. A third-party logo is not independent verification. Confirm that the laboratory exists, that its contact details and accreditation claims are real, and that the report can be checked through the laboratory rather than only through the vendor. A verification code, QR destination, or report lookup controlled by the issuing laboratory is a meaningful signal.

Finally, consider sample custody. Who selected the vial? Was it taken from the sellable lot? Was the sample sealed? A sophisticated instrument cannot correct a weak link between the analysed sample and the inventory presented to researchers.

One number cannot answer every question

Identity

Mass spectrometry is commonly used to assess whether the molecular mass is consistent with the claimed peptide. Identity is foundational: a high-purity result for the wrong compound is still the wrong compound.

Chromatographic purity

HPLC or a coupled LC method separates detectable components and reports the relative area associated with the target peak under the stated conditions. This can support a purity claim, but it does not automatically prove identity and it does not necessarily tell you how much of the vial’s total powder mass is active peptide.

Net content

Water, salts, counterions, residual solvents, and other non-peptide mass may contribute to the total weight. A vial can show high chromatographic purity while containing less peptide mass than its headline fill claim implies. Content or assay testing addresses that different question.

Contaminants and microbiological attributes

Residual synthesis reagents, endotoxin, bioburden, sterility, heavy metals, and particulate matter require their own methods. “99% purity” is not a substitute for these measurements. A sterile result also does not establish low endotoxin, because endotoxin can remain after living organisms are absent.

The raw output matters

A chromatogram shows the separation produced by the instrument: peaks, retention times, integration boundaries, and baseline behaviour. A mass spectrum shows the detected mass-to-charge signals. These outputs are not infallible, but they allow an informed reviewer to see what supports the summary table.

Review the method name, instrument, sample preparation statement, acceptance criteria, and any deviations. Ask whether the integration looks plausible and whether the report explains how identity was assigned. A single screenshot without axes, method, or sample ID is not equivalent to a signed analytical package.

What weak or fabricated documentation looks like

  • no laboratory address, contact route, or verifiable existence;
  • no lot number, or a lot that does not match the vial;
  • the same report used for multiple lots or products;
  • no test date, method, signature, or authorisation;
  • a verification link that returns only to the vendor’s own website;
  • summary values with no chromatogram, spectrum, or supporting output;
  • identical “perfect” results across every product and batch;
  • a current product paired with an old certificate and no continuity evidence;
  • claims of identity, content, sterility, and endotoxin control inferred from one HPLC purity number.

A five-step COA audit

1 · MatchCompare product, concentration, lot, and date to the vial.
2 · VerifyConfirm the issuing laboratory and report outside the vendor’s site.
3 · SeparateIdentify which results address identity, purity, content, and contaminants.
4 · InspectReview chromatograms, spectra, methods, limits, and signatures.
5 · DecideDocument release, quarantine, retest, or rejection.
RecordPreserve the report with the study and inventory history.

A good COA does not ask for trust. It gives a researcher a path to verification. The strongest vendors make that path easier: current lot, identifiable laboratory, relevant methods, visible raw data, and a lookup mechanism the seller cannot quietly rewrite.
